reviewer: Codex deut_1_3 (AI-assisted supplied-English curation for 1 Kings 14–18)
review_method: Read all155 complete actual source units:85 in14–16 and70 in17–18, including every actual gap and continuation and chapter14's start at14:21. Read all retained complete targets and necessary contexts, including all actual2Chronicles12–17,20:31–37/21:1, Genesis35:9–12, Joshua6:26, Deuteronomy18:9–12,2Kings4:32–35/17:10, Luke4:24–27/7:11–17, James5:16–18,2Chronicles7:1–3 and the relevant1Kings11:34–36/11:38/12:24k–24n/12:28–30/19:1–2/20:17–24 contexts. Separately reread every155 complete source/target/category/rationale triple in four untruncated groups1–40,41–80,81–120,121–155. Preserved the exact original draft and fourteen coherent literal-wording refinements; separately reread all fourteen complete final changed triples. Retained links use particular narrative promises and stated outcomes, explicit later recollections, bounded parallel/contrasting regnal notices and meaningful labelled local literary dependencies. Unresolved dates, parentage, names and voyage reconstructions receive zero credit; a retained bounded comparison does not solve its excluded harmonization proposal. This is an initial curated supplied-English pass, not exhaustive discovery, new Greek/Hebrew/apparatus work, specialist approval or independently certified chronology, modern geography or technical translation.
pin_method: Fresh fixed-commit raw fetches of all8 source/target books, exact Git blob rehash against the immutable registry and complete parsed-cache equality. Byte normalization differences recorded separately; inventory and technical checks add zero review credit.

old_row.relationship: Pillars and groves on high hills and under leafy trees
old_row.rationale: Both describe setting up pillars or standing stones and groves on high hills and beneath shady or leafy trees. Kings' high-place clause and the different regnal settings are not silently transferred between the notices.

new_row.relationship: Pillars and groves on high hills and under leafy trees
new_row.rationale: Both describe setting up pillars or standing stones and groves on high hills and beneath shady or leafy trees. The source's additional high-place clause and the different regnal settings are not silently transferred between the notices.

old_row.relationship: Silver, gold and vessels are brought into the Lord’s house with different object labels
old_row.rationale: Kings brings paternal and personal pillars, silver, gold and vessels into the Lord's house; Chronicles brings holy things with silver, gold and vessels. Pillars are not silently renamed holy things, and Chronicles' explicit David wording remains its own detail.

new_row.relationship: Silver, gold and vessels are brought into the Lord’s house with different object labels
new_row.rationale: Kings brings his father's and his own pillars—silver and gold pillars—and vessels into the Lord's house; Chronicles brings holy things with silver, gold and vessels. Pillars are not silently renamed holy things, and Chronicles' explicit David wording remains its own detail.

old_row.relationship: Ramah’s stones and timber are reused with different destination descriptions
old_row.rationale: Both take Ramah's stones and timber through Asa's Judah levy and reuse them. Kings says the whole hill of Benjamin and watchtower; Chronicles names Gabae and Maspha. Those descriptions and the Ainakim extent are not independently normalized.

new_row.relationship: Ramah’s stones and timber are reused with different destination descriptions
new_row.rationale: Both accounts have Asa involve Judah and take Ramah's stones and timber for further building. Kings says the whole hill of Benjamin and watchtower; Chronicles names Gabae and Maspha. Those descriptions and the Ainakim extent are not independently normalized.

old_row.relationship: Same-chapter The Jehu-Hanani word introduction recurs in the extended charge
old_row.rationale: Both units name the Lord's word through Jehu son of Hanani against Baasha. The later repetition adds reasons and an unresolved it clause, rather than supplying a new prophet identity or independently assigning that pronoun.

new_row.relationship: Same-chapter The Jehu-Hanani word introduction recurs in the extended charge
new_row.rationale: Both notices name Jehu son of Hanani, the Lord's speech and Baasha. The introduction says the word came to Baasha; the later notice expressly speaks against Baasha and his house, with additional reasons and an it clause whose object is not independently reassigned.

old_row.relationship: Same-chapter The extended Baasha charge repeats the same named prophetic introduction
old_row.rationale: The later notice names Jehu son of Hanani and the Lord speaking against Baasha's house, as the opening does. Its hand-work and it clauses stay as supplied without independently deciding every object or motive.

new_row.relationship: Same-chapter The extended Baasha charge repeats the same named prophetic introduction
new_row.rationale: The later notice names Jehu son of Hanani and the Lord's charge against Baasha and his house; the opening introduces the Lord's word through that same named prophet to Baasha. The added hand-work and it clauses stay as supplied without independently deciding every object or motive.

old_row.relationship: Same-chapter The half-cavalry commander’s conspiracy is followed by the narrated strike
old_row.rationale: Zimri, commander of half the cavalry, conspires while Elah is drunk at Osa's house; the next unit records Zimri striking, killing and succeeding. Cavalry is not changed into chariots, and no unreported weapon is added.

new_row.relationship: Same-chapter The half-cavalry commander’s conspiracy is followed by the narrated strike
new_row.rationale: Zimri, commander of half the cavalry, conspires; the unit includes drinking in Tirzah at Osa's house, and the next unit names Zimri's striking, killing and succeeding. old_row.relationship: Same-chapter The Baasha-Elah sin summary repeats the divine charge’s provoking language
old_row.rationale: The closure names Baasha and Elah causing Israel to sin with worthless things; the earlier divine charge says Baasha caused God's people to sin and provoked Him with worthless things. The added son remains the later summary's detail.

new_row.relationship: Same-chapter The Baasha-Elah sin summary repeats the divine charge’s provoking language
new_row.rationale: The closure names Baasha and Elah's sins and uses causing-Israel-to-sin and worthless-things language; the earlier divine charge expressly addresses Baasha causing God's people to sin. The later singular causing-sin pronoun is not independently assigned to both men.

old_row.relationship: Same-chapter Omri’s named hill-building account beside his Samaria burial notice
old_row.rationale: Omri buys Shemer's hill and names his building Saemeron; the later closure buries Omri in Samaria. The particular city-building and burial sequence retains Semeron, Saemeron and Samaria without a newly certified place equation or modern map.

new_row.relationship: Same-chapter Omri’s named hill-building account beside his Samaria burial notice
new_row.rationale: Omri buys Shemer's hill and names the hill he built on Saemeron; the later closure buries Omri in Samaria. The particular hill-building and burial sequence retains Semeron, Saemeron and Samaria without a newly certified place equation or modern map.

old_row.relationship: Same-chapter Ahab son of Omri follows Omri’s burial and succession notice

new_row.relationship: Same-chapter Ahab son of Omri follows Omri’s burial and succession notice

old_row.relationship: Jehoshaphat’s unsuccessful ship project has a parallel with distinct destinations and partnership clauses
old_row.rationale: Kings' single Tarshish ship for Sophir's gold is wrecked at Ezion-geber; Chronicles' ships for Tharsis are wrecked in the Gasion-gaber project. The singular/plural, destination and alliance notices are preserved without a single reconstructed voyage.

new_row.relationship: Jehoshaphat’s unsuccessful ship project has a parallel with distinct destinations and partnership clauses
new_row.rationale: Kings' single Tarshish ship for Sophir's gold is wrecked at Ezion-geber; Chronicles has ships built at Gasion-gaber and reports their wrecking and inability to go to Tharsis. The singular/plural, destination, building-place and alliance notices are preserved without a single reconstructed voyage.

unresolved_candidates.status: pending proposed regnal duration and maternal parentage harmonization; no identity or reconciliation credit
unresolved_candidates.reason: Kings gives six years and Maacah daughter of Absalom; Chronicles gives three years and Maacah daughter of Ouriel from Gabaon. The retained comparison concerns the corresponding Judah regnal framework in Jeroboam's eighteenth-year context, not a solved date or parentage.

unresolved_candidates.status: pending proposed Asa reign length and death date harmonization; no identity or reconciliation credit
unresolved_candidates.reason: Kings gives Asa forty-one years in Jerusalem; Chronicles dates his death to the thirty-ninth regnal year. Both actual notices were read. No corrected numeral, co-regency or calendar solution is claimed; the retained pair displays the explicit contrast.

unresolved_candidates.status: pending proposed maternal identity and removed function harmonization; no identity or reconciliation credit
unresolved_candidates.reason: Kings names Ana his mother, removal from leadership following her grove gathering, and burned hiding places at Kidron. Chronicles names Maacah his mother, Astarte ministry, and a burned idol at Kedron. The retained removal-and-burning parallel does not certify the women's identity, replace mother with grandmother, or equate each function and object.

unresolved_candidates.status: pending proposed shipping actor and voyage chronology harmonization; no identity or reconciliation credit
unresolved_candidates.reason: Kings' unnamed Israel king offers attendants and young men, and Jehoshaphat is unwilling. Chronicles names an actual partnership with Ahaziah to make ships. The retained shipping comparison preserves the contrasting clauses without assigning the anonymous king Ahaziah's name or declaring the offer accepted or the projects one voyage.

unresolved_candidates.status: pending proposed Hiel and Ozan personal identity harmonization; no identity or reconciliation credit
unresolved_candidates.reason: Kings names Hiel of Bethel, Abiram and Segub and explicitly cites Joshua's foundation-and-gates word. Joshua gives the curse and an Ozan of Bethel example with Abiram and an unnamed youngest surviving son. The retained explicit curse connection does not independently certify Hiel equals Ozan or supply Segub's name to Joshua.

candidate_exclusions.proposed_claim: Harmonize differing regnal dates, mother names and parentage, tribal/place forms, shipping actors and chronology; translate nasib or replace Syria with Edom; assign ambiguous drinking/causing-sin pronouns; import familiar cult labels, time totals, medical mechanisms, geometric measures, a hand-shaped cloud or a chariot-riding action.
candidate_exclusions.reason: Only bounded actual clauses are retained. Every unsupported identity, technical gloss and numerical/historical reconstruction remains uncredited.

editorial_notes.note: Preserve six years, the twenty-fourth Jeroboam year, Ana as mother, silver/gold pillars, the cave, cavalry, Thamni's brother Joram, all16:28a–h, the literal Syria—nasib notice, singular ship and unwillingness, both Hiel/Ozan forms, plural children, morning bread/evening meat, three breathings and child cried out, Obadiah's burned-kingdom claim as speech, utterly alone alongside the hundred hidden, the prophets' and people's different movements, the backward-heart clause, two metretes of seed, cloud like a man's footprint, and Ahab wept. No Scripture wording or preserved source field is revised.
